14	CASE OD2-DEV2-SEQ (SEQ, organizational): Hollin Vale Bank: small-business loan approvals nearly double
15	Setting: Hollin Vale Bank is a fictional regional lender with 19 branches across the Maddern Valley. Branch loan officers take in small-business (SME) loan applications and collect the documents. All SME credit decisions are made centrally by the Credit Hub in Kestwick. In the second quarter the bank moved to a new loan-origination system (Corvane Origination), renewed its contract with its only valuation panel firm, refreshed its credit policy, and replaced five departing SME loan officers.
16	Presenting request: The COO wants to know why SME loan approvals have taken longer since the spring and what the bank should do. Her month-end decision paper covers the Corvane contract and the performance of the new hires.
17	INITIAL EVIDENCE
18	E1 [stage S1] Email from Imogen Raye, COO, to the executive team, 1 September (leadership-account): Subject: SME approvals. Since we switched to Corvane in April, our small-business approval times have nearly doubled: 13 days in August against 7 in March. On top of that we lost five experienced loan officers in Q2, and the replacements are still learning. By month-end I want two things. First, a decision paper on whether we withhold Corvane's final milestone payment and go back to the legacy workflow. Second, a plan from HR, with targets, to get the new hires up to speed. Customers are noticing, and withdrawals are up too.
19	E2 [stage S1] Monthly lending dashboard, SME loans, March–August (system-record): Median business days from application to decision, Mar–Aug: 7.2, 8.0, 9.6, 11.8, 13.1, 13.4. Applications received: 212, 205, 219, 224, 231, 228. Withdrawn before decision: 6.1%, 6.4%, 7.0%, 8.2%, 8.9%, 8.5%. Consumer loans (same branches, on Corvane since April), median days: 3.9, 4.6, 4.2, 4.0, 4.1, 4.0. The SME median rose at 18 of 19 branches. Footnote: since the Corvane cutover (14 April), SME applications with no customer document upload for 30 calendar days are auto-closed and counted as withdrawn. The legacy system left such files open indefinitely.
20	E3 [stage S1] HR summary for the COO, 22 August (document): SME loan officers: 34 at 1 April. Leavers April–June: 5 (3 retirements, 2 resignations to a competitor), average tenure 14 years. Replacements started between 6 May and 17 June at Ashby North, Brenmoor, Calder Quay, Hythe Lane and Overstrand. Two are internal transfers from consumer lending. All five completed the three-week Corvane and credit-procedures induction. Headcount was back to 34 by 17 June. Branch lending authorities are unchanged: the Credit Hub still makes all SME credit decisions centrally.
21	E4 [stage S1] Interview notes, Dev Okafor, Brenmoor branch manager, 26 August (manager-account): 'Corvane was painful in April. We were scanning everything twice and logins kept dropping. That's mostly settled now. The real problem starts once a file goes to the Hub. The status just says "With Credit Hub", it sits there a week or more, and then it comes back approved. Nobody tells us what they're doing. My new officer is fine on paperwork; on the system she's quicker than the man she replaced.' Asked whether all SME files are affected equally: 'Feels like it, but I haven't checked.'
22	E5 [stage S1] Operations change calendar, Q2 (extract) (change-record): 1 Apr – Valuation panel contract renewed with Pellow & Strand Valuers (sole panel firm). New fee schedule; service levels unchanged. 14 Apr – Corvane Origination goes live at all branches for consumer and SME lending. 1 May – Credit Policy v14 takes effect (annual refresh). Credit Policy Unit note: 'Largely editorial; no change to approval authorities or pricing.' 6 May–17 Jun – five replacement SME loan officers start (see HR summary). 3 Jun – one Credit Hub SME underwriter goes on parental leave; a contractor covers until November.
23	CATALOGUE (full contents)
24	C1 [stage S1] Corvane stage timestamps, decided SME loans, March–August - Corvane management-information report, run by the Credit Hub analyst (system-record): Median business days per workflow stage. Columns Mar|Apr|Jun|Aug; March is reconstructed from legacy timestamps. Stages run in sequence: underwriting cannot start until any required valuation report has arrived. The branch status 'With Credit Hub' covers valuation, underwriting and decision. Property-secured loans (55–58% of decisions): intake 1.3|1.9|1.4|1.3; document collection 2.3|2.7|2.4|2.4; collateral valuation (requested to report received) 1.6|1.7|7.6|8.4; underwriting 2.1|2.2|2.2|2.3; decision 0.6|0.6|0.7|0.6; sum 7.9|9.1|14.3|15.0. Unsecured loans: intake 1.2|1.8|1.3|1.2; document collection 2.0|2.4|2.1|2.1; underwriting 1.9|2.0|2.0|2.1; decision 0.5|0.5|0.5|0.5; sum 5.6|6.7|5.9|5.9. Document collection at the five branches with Q2 hires was 2.4 in March and 2.4 in August, against 2.3 and 2.3 elsewhere.
25	C2 [stage S1] Collateral valuation order register, March–August - Credit Hub valuation desk order register (system-record): Property-secured SME applications, Mar|Apr|May|Jun|Jul|Aug. Orders: 112|108|121|118|124|119. Full appraisals: 31|29|74|79|83|80. Desktop valuations: 81|79|47|39|41|39. Median days from valuation requested in Corvane to order placed with Pellow & Strand: 0.3 every month. Median firm turnaround for full appraisals: 8.6|8.4|8.8|8.7|8.9|8.6; for desktop valuations: 1.2|1.1|1.2|1.2|1.2|1.1. Loans above $500k had full appraisals throughout; their valuation stage was 8.5 days in March and 8.7 in August. From 2 May, every order for exposures between $150k and $500k carries the code 'POL14-6.3 full appraisal mandatory'. Before May, this band was valued by desktop. Orders under $150k are still desktop valuations.
26	C3 [stage S1] Credit Policy v13 to v14 clause-change list - Credit Policy Unit (document): 23 clauses changed. 19 are wording, cross-reference or renumbering changes. §4.2: KYC document list updated (adds a beneficial-ownership form already collected in practice). §5.7: pricing grid reference updated. §6.3: mandatory full (inspection) appraisal of property collateral now applies to exposures above $150k (previously above $500k); desktop valuation is still permitted below that. Rationale: internal audit finding IA-23-11 found that desktop valuations of owner-occupied commercial premises exceeded later full appraisals by a median 12%. §8.1: delegated authority table reformatted, limits unchanged. Effective 1 May. Impact assessment on processing times: 'not assessed'.
27	C4 [stage S1] Pellow & Strand quarterly service review letter, Q2 - Account director, Pellow & Strand Valuers, 15 July (vendor-account): 'Q2 service-level compliance for Hollin Vale was 97% (Q1: 99%). Two late reports in June were caused by access delays at borrower premises. Given the change in instruction mix, we would welcome a review of the fee schedule. We remain committed to our 10-business-day standard for full appraisals.'
28	C5 [stage S1] Exit interview summaries, five departed SME loan officers - HR business partner (staff-account): Exit interviews, April–June. The three retirees describe their retirements as planned; one says, 'Corvane training came too late for me to bother.' The two who left for Tremont Mutual cite pay (+9%) and hybrid working. Four of the five rate their branch manager 'good' or 'very good'. None mentions credit policy or valuations. One says the Hub 'has always been slow on anything with property attached.'
29	C6 [stage S1] Induction and training completion records, Q2 SME hires - Learning and development team (document): Learning records for the five Q2 SME hires. Corvane SME module: 5/5 complete (scores 82–96%). Credit procedures v14: 5/5 complete. KYC refresher: 5/5 complete. Shadowing days with an experienced officer: 4, 6, 5, 3 and 5 (target 5). Two hires are internal transfers with 4 and 7 years in consumer lending. Training coordinator's note: 'All cleared to originate independently by 1 July.'
30	C7 [stage S1] Corvane service-desk ticket log, 14 April–31 August - Corvane Systems service desk export (log): Tickets raised by Hollin Vale users: April (from the 14th) 46, May 18, June 11, July 9, August 12. Categories: document scanning or duplicate upload 31; login or session timeout 22; reporting 17; workflow routing 16; other 10. A scanning defect was patched on 20 May. Open at 31 August: 3 tickets, all workflow routing. One reads 'branch users cannot see the sub-status of files with Credit Hub' (priority: medium).
31	C8 [stage S1] Credit Hub SME underwriter roster and caseload, March–August - Credit Hub team lead (system-record): SME underwriting team: 6 FTE March–May; from 3 June, 5 permanent staff plus 1 contractor. Files entering underwriting per underwriter per month: Mar 35, Apr 34, May 36, Jun 37, Jul 39, Aug 38. The contractor handled 24–29 files a month in the first two months (team average 37). Overtime hours: Q1 44, Q2 51. Team lead's comment: 'We're stretched but keeping up.'
32	C9 [stage S1] Withdrawn SME applications: closure reason codes, May–August - Corvane closure-code extract (system-record): SME applications closed without a decision, May–August (n=73). Auto-closed after 30 days with no customer document upload: 32. Customer withdrew – financed elsewhere: 14. Customer withdrew – project cancelled or deferred: 12. Customer withdrew – no reason given: 11. Branch closed – duplicate application: 4. The legacy system did not record closure reasons, so there is no pre-April comparison. Of the 14 'financed elsewhere' cases, 8 were property-secured.
33	C10 [stage S1] SME customer complaints log, March–August - Customer relations team (customer-account): SME lending complaints: Mar 4, Apr 9, May 7, Jun 11, Jul 14, Aug 15. Main themes, June–August: no progress updates while the file is 'with the bank' (19); asked for the same document twice (6); valuation fee higher than expected (7); relationship manager changed (4); other (4). Sample, August: 'Told it was with head office for ten days and nobody could say why.'
34	C11 [stage S1] Branch lending staff pulse survey, July - People analytics team (anonymous-staff-survey): Quarterly pulse survey of branch lending staff, July (71% response). 'I have the tools to do my job': 52% agree (January: 68%). 'Corvane makes my work easier': 31% agree. 'I understand why SME files take as long as they do': 24% agree. Free-text themes: Corvane screens (41 mentions), Hub communication (33), workload after colleagues left (18), policy changes (5).
35	C12 [stage S1] Regional peer benchmark of SME decision times, first half-year - Regional lenders' benchmarking consortium (external-data): First-half report, 7 regional lenders, anonymised. Median SME application-to-decision time: 8.5 business days (second half of last year: 8.3). Range 5.9–12.4. Hollin Vale, first half: 8.7. Note: participants define start and end points differently, and secured and unsecured loans are not reported separately.
36	C13 [stage S1] Conduct supervisor's letter on SME lending, June - Regional conduct supervisor, circular to all lenders, 12 June (regulator-record): The letter reminds lenders to tell small-business applicants clearly how long a decision is expected to take and what fees they will be charged, including third-party valuation costs. It asks for complaint volumes by year end. It contains no findings specific to Hollin Vale and sets no deadline for changes to processes.
37	C14 [stage S1] Interview notes, four further branch managers - COO's office, interviews 27–29 August (manager-account): Ashby North: 'Corvane slowed everything in spring, and new staff need more hand-holding.' Hythe Lane: 'Files sit with the Hub. The underwriters have been short-handed since June.' Pendle Cross: 'No new hires here and we're slower too, so I don't buy the staffing story.' Overstrand: 'Customers complain about not knowing where things are. I assume the Hub is swamped.' None of the four had looked at stage-level data.
38	C15 [stage S1] SME lending income and fee summary, Q1–Q2 - Finance business partner, retail lending (financial-record): SME net interest income, Q2 against Q1: +3%. Arrangement fee income: flat. Valuation fees are passed through to applicants in full and do not appear in bank income. SME loan book balance: +2.1% over the quarter. Provisions charge: unchanged. Finance note: 'No material P&L effect visible yet from longer processing times.'
39	CANDIDATES
40	H1: The main driver of the longer SME approval times is the loss of experienced loan officers and their replacement by new hires.
41	H2: The main driver of the longer SME approval times is the April migration to the new loan-origination system.
42	H3: The main driver of the longer SME approval times is a change to credit policy requirements that took effect during the second quarter.
43	H4: The main driver of the longer SME approval times is slower turnaround by the bank's external valuation firm.
44	H5: The longer approval times are causing more small-business applicants to abandon their applications.
45	H6: The main driver of the longer SME approval times is higher application volume combined with reduced underwriting capacity at the Credit Hub.
46	R1: Credit Policy v14 refresh (effective 1 May) -> Longer collateral-valuation stage for property-secured SME loans (causes)
47	R2: Longer SME approval times -> Higher share of SME applications withdrawn before decision (causes)
48	R3: Corvane go-live (14 April) -> Sustained rise in SME approval times from May onward (causes)
49	R4: Valuation panel contract renewal (1 April) -> Longer collateral-valuation stage for property-secured SME loans (causes)
50	A1: Ask the credit risk committee to decide whether to amend the collateral-valuation provisions of the May credit policy refresh, presenting the measured delay alongside the policy's risk rationale.
51	A2: Put the SME loan officers hired in Q2 on performance-improvement plans with approval-time targets.
52	A3: Launch a fee-rebate offer for small-business applicants to win back customers lost to slower approvals.
53	A4: Withhold Corvane's final milestone payment and instruct the vendor to restore the legacy SME approval workflow.
54	A5: Add a by-stage breakdown of SME approval times to the monthly management dashboard.

answers.justification: Document collection at the five branches with new hires was flat (2.4 in March and August, C1). The median rose at 18 of 19 branches, including Pendle Cross, which had no new hires (E2, C14). The hires were fully trained (C6, E4).

Corvane caused only a temporary bump in April: intake and document collection, and all unsecured stages, went back to baseline (C1). Consumer loans on the same system stayed flat (E2), and Corvane tickets fell after the 20 May patch (C7).

Policy v14 §6.3 lowered the full-appraisal threshold from $500k to $150k from 1 May (C3). Orders coded 'POL14-6.3' moved the $150k–500k band from desktop to full appraisals (31 to roughly 80 a month), each taking about 8.6 days (C2). The valuation stage rose from 1.6 to 8.4 days while every other stage stayed flat (C1).

Pellow & Strand's turnaround for each valuation type was unchanged: full appraisals 8.4–8.9 days, desktop about 1.2 (C2). Loans over $500k kept a stable valuation stage (8.5 to 8.7 days), and the bank placed orders in 0.3 days every month (C2). Service compliance was 97% (C4).

Withdrawals rose (E2), but an auto-close rule introduced with Corvane on 14 April now counts stalled files as withdrawn (E2). That rule accounts for 32 of 73 closures, and there are no pre-April reason codes to compare against (C9). Property-secured loans are not over-represented among 'financed elsewhere' cases (8 of 14, C9).

Volume rose only about 7% (E2) and the caseload per underwriter rose modestly (C8). The underwriting stage stayed flat at 2.1–2.3 days, and unsecured loans that go through the same underwriters were not slower (C1).

All the elements are present: the timing (policy effective 1 May, coded orders from 2 May), a mechanism (full appraisals take about 8.6 days versus 1.2 for desktop), and the shift in valuation mix (C2, C3). Main rivals are ruled out: firm turnaround and the over-$500k control group were stable, and order placement was unchanged (C2, C1).

The withdrawal share rose alongside approval times (E2), but the new 30-day auto-close rule confounds the measure and there is no pre-April reason-code baseline (C9). So the evidence shows co-occurrence, not causation.

Corvane's effect was confined to April. From May onward, the sustained rise appears only in the valuation stage of property-secured loans. Unsecured SME and consumer times on Corvane went back to baseline (C1, E2).

The renewal changed fees, not service levels (E5). The firm's turnaround for each valuation type was unchanged after renewal, and the valuation stage stayed flat in April after the 1 April renewal (C2, C1).

It targets the cause that has been identified (C1, C2, C3) and puts the delay against the risk rationale from internal audit IA-23-11 (C3). Leaving the decision to the risk committee is appropriate, rather than unilaterally reversing a control.
The new hires' stage times match those of other branches (C1). They are fully trained (C6) and do not make credit decisions (E3), so performance plans would punish the wrong people.
It depends on H5, which is still unestablished (E2, C9), and it does not address the delay caused by valuations. Valuation fees are also passed through to applicants (C15).

Corvane is not driving the sustained delay (C1, E2). Withholding payment and restoring the legacy workflow would punish the wrong vendor, cause disruption, and lose stage-level visibility that only Corvane provides (C1).

A stage breakdown would have revealed the valuation bottleneck that the headline dashboard hid (E2, C1), and it would address the visibility complaints (C10, C11). It is a useful complement, but it is monitoring rather than the main fix.

Stage timestamps, the valuation order register and the policy clause list together pin down the cause and rule out the rivals (C1, C2, C3). That is enough to put the policy trade-off to the credit risk committee (A1).
